trees.q: What does Gini impurity measure for a group of rows in a decision tree?
options: How evenly the rows are spread across the feature values
How mixed the class labels are, from 0 for a pure group upward
How many splits are needed to reach a leaf
How much the tree's accuracy improves on test data
trees.why: Gini is 0 when every row shares one class and rises as the classes mix, reaching 0.5 for a 50/50 two-class group.

trees.q: How does a random forest differ from plain bagging of decision trees?
options: It trains trees in sequence on the previous errors
It uses only one shallow tree per feature
Each split considers a random subset of the features
It removes the bootstrap sampling step entirely
trees.why: Random forests keep bootstrap samples and add random feature choice at each split, which makes the trees less alike. Training in sequence on errors is boosting.

trees.q: A client's tree scores 100% on training data and 81% on new data. What do you try first?
options: Limit depth or raise min_samples_leaf and tune with cross-validation
Add more features so the tree can split even further
Report the training score since it shows the model's full ability
Switch the impurity measure from Gini to entropy
trees.why: The large gap means the tree memorised noise. Pruning through depth or leaf size, tuned on validation folds, is the direct fix; changing Gini to entropy rarely matters.

trees.q: A risk team must read and audit every rule, but also wants the best scores. What do you propose?
options: One unlimited-depth tree for both jobs
A random forest, with its impurity importances as the rules
A pruned shallow tree to explain, plus a forest or boosted model to score
A kNN model, since neighbours are easy to show
trees.why: A shallow pruned tree gives readable rules, while an ensemble gives stronger scores; disagreements can go to human review.

trees.q: Spot the mistake: 'customer_id ranks second in feature_importances_, so IDs drive churn.'
options: Nothing, importance always reflects real causes
Impurity importance favours many-valued columns like IDs; check permutation importance
The ranking is wrong because trees ignore numeric columns
IDs matter, but only after scaling them first
trees.why: Impurity importance is biased toward high-cardinality features and is measured on training data. Permutation importance on held-out data shows an ID adds nothing.

boosting.q: In gradient boosting, what is each new tree trained to predict?
options: The original target, using a fresh bootstrap sample
The errors (residuals or gradients) of the model so far
The feature that has the highest importance
The average of all previous trees' predictions
boosting.why: Each round fits a small tree to what the current model still gets wrong, then adds it in scaled by the learning rate.

boosting.q: What usually happens if you lower the learning rate from 0.3 to 0.03 and keep the same number of trees?
options: The model overfits much faster
Training becomes unstable and diverges
The model may underfit because it needs many more trees
Nothing, the learning rate only affects speed
boosting.why: Smaller steps need more rounds to reach the same fit. Use early stopping or raise the number of trees when you lower the rate.

boosting.q: A shipper wants to predict next week's late deliveries. How should you split data for early stopping?
options: A random 15% of all rows, shuffled
The most recent weeks as validation, with an even later period for the test
Use the test set for early stopping to save data
No validation set, just use 1,000 trees
boosting.why: For time-ordered problems, validation and test data must come after the training period, or the model sees the future and scores look too good.

boosting.q: Operations asks why a single order was flagged by your boosted model. What do you show?
options: The global feature importance bar chart
The model's total number of trees
SHAP values for that order, turned into plain reasons
The learning rate and max depth settings
boosting.why: SHAP gives per-row contributions that add up to that prediction, which answers 'why this one'. Global importance only says what matters on average.

boosting.q: Spot the mistake: 'SHAP shows region adds +0.4 to risk, so moving depots out of that region will cut delays.'
options: SHAP explains the model's use of a feature, not cause and effect
SHAP values cannot be positive for classification
SHAP only works for linear models
The value should be divided by the learning rate first
boosting.why: A large contribution means the model relies on the feature. Whether changing it changes outcomes needs causal evidence such as an experiment.

knnsvm.q: How does kNN classify a new row?
options: It fits a line and checks which side the row is on
It finds the k most similar training rows and takes a vote
It multiplies word probabilities for each class
It builds k trees and averages them
knnsvm.why: kNN stores training rows and predicts from the majority of the k nearest ones by distance.

knnsvm.q: In an SVM, what are support vectors?
options: The training points nearest the boundary that define it
The features with the largest weights
Extra columns created by the kernel
Rows the model classified wrongly on test data
knnsvm.why: Only the points closest to the margin decide where the boundary lies; moving other points does not change it.

knnsvm.q: A kNN model on income in dollars and age in years ignores age. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: k is too small; raise k to 50
Age has too few values; drop it
Features are unscaled; add StandardScaler in a Pipeline
Distances are wrong; switch to Naive Bayes
knnsvm.why: Income's large range dominates Euclidean distance. Scaling inside a pipeline gives both features fair weight without leaking test data.

knnsvm.q: A help desk needs a ticket router this week and has 300 labelled tickets. What do you build first?
options: A kernel SVM on raw text characters
Word counts with Multinomial Naive Bayes as a baseline
kNN on ticket length and hour sent
A deep neural network trained from scratch
knnsvm.why: Naive Bayes on counts trains in seconds, works with few labels and is easy to inspect, so it is a strong first baseline to beat.

knnsvm.q: Spot the mistake: 'Test accuracy dropped, so we raised RBF gamma to 100 to fit the data more closely.'
options: gamma only affects training speed
High gamma makes each point's influence tiny and tends to overfit
gamma must always equal C
RBF kernels ignore gamma when data is scaled
knnsvm.why: Large gamma gives wiggly boundaries that hug training points, which usually lowers test accuracy further. Tune gamma and C with cross-validation.

clustering.q: What are the two steps k-means repeats until it converges?
options: Split and prune
Assign points to the nearest center, then move centers to their points' mean
Merge the two closest clusters, then redraw the tree
Label dense points as core, then mark others as noise
clustering.why: k-means alternates assign and update. Merging is hierarchical clustering; core and noise points are DBSCAN.

clustering.q: What does a silhouette score near 0 for a point mean?
options: The point sits near the border between two clusters
The point is exactly at its cluster center
The point is noise and will be removed
The clustering has perfect separation
clustering.why: Silhouette compares distance to the own cluster with distance to the nearest other; near 0 means both are about equal.

clustering.q: A retailer's k-means gives one segment of 40 huge buyers and one of everyone else. What do you do first?
options: Increase k to 20 until segments look even
Log-transform and scale features, and handle extreme accounts separately
Switch to Naive Bayes
Report the two segments as found
clustering.why: Skewed, unscaled spend lets a few extreme rows dominate distances. Log, scale and a rule for outliers usually give usable segments.

clustering.q: Fraud analysts want to find odd transactions and groups of any shape, with no k known. Which method fits?
options: k-means with k=2
Hierarchical clustering with single linkage and no scaling
DBSCAN, which labels sparse points as noise
Linear regression on the transaction amount
clustering.why: DBSCAN needs no k, finds clusters of any shape and marks isolated points with -1, which is useful for spotting outliers.

clustering.q: Spot the mistake: 'We picked k=9 because it had the lowest inertia of all k we tried.'
options: Inertia always falls as k grows, so lowest inertia just favours the largest k
Inertia should be maximised, not minimised
k-means cannot use more than 8 clusters
Inertia is only valid for DBSCAN
clustering.why: More clusters always reduce inertia. Use the elbow, silhouette, stability and business needs to choose k.
